title: Commas
intro: Learn where a comma helps—and where it splits words that belong together.

sections.heading: Common jobs of a comma
body: Use a comma plus a connecting word such as and or but to join two complete thoughts. A comma also separates an introductory clause, phrase, or word. Paired commas enclose extra information. Other commas separate list items or two adjectives that each describe the same noun.
Commas also introduce many quotations and mark direct address: “Maya, bring your notes.” Do not insert a lone comma between subject and verb or verb and object just because you pause there.

examples.text: My alarm did not go off, so I arrived late.
examples.label: Job 1: comma + FANBOYS joining two independent clauses

examples.text: While electronic music is popular, many people still prefer rock.
examples.label: Job 2: opening dependent clause + independent clause

examples.text: The team's strongest swimmer, broke the school record.
examples.label: Wrong: this comma splits subject and verb

sections.tip: For an opening phrase, check the boundary: 'After a long day at school, Maya rested.' The phrase is introductory even though it has no subject and verb.

sections.heading: Unnecessary information commas
body: Cover the extra information and reread. If the sentence stays complete and still identifies the same person or thing, that information is nonessential: useful extra detail that can be set off with commas.
If removal changes which person or thing is meant, keep the information without commas. A nonessential interruption in the middle needs both opening and closing commas.

examples.text: Mrs. Ellison, who is known for pop quizzes, is my least favorite teacher.
examples.label: Non-essential: commas on both sides

examples.text: The dresses that need to be hemmed are hanging in the closet.
examples.label: Essential: no commas (tells which dresses)

examples.text: The snowboard in the closet, the one with no stickers, needs waxing.
examples.label: Non-essential aside, walled off by a pair of commas

sections.tip: Cross it out. If the sentence still stands and means the same thing, wrap the phrase in commas. If not, use no commas.

sections.heading: The Names Rule
body: Ask whether the name identifies the person or adds detail about someone already identified. “My friend Kelly” can need the name to say which friend.

“The museum’s only curator, Lena Ortiz,” already identifies one person. An added description also takes commas: “Kelly, my friend from London, visits.” Context decides; position or a title alone does not.

examples.text: Italian cyclist Marco Pantani won the Tour de France in 1998.
examples.label: Generic description fits many people: no commas

examples.text: The museum’s only curator, Lena Ortiz, opened the exhibit.
examples.label: Description fits only one person: commas around the name

examples.text: Kelly, my friend from London, visits every summer.
examples.label: Extra description after an identified name: commas

sections.tip: Use context: is the name needed to identify the person? If yes, no commas. If the person is already identified, set off the extra name.

sections.heading: Listing commas
body: Separate three or more list items with commas. The final serial comma before and is a style choice unless clarity requires it. Two ordinary items joined by and do not need a comma; if and joins complete thoughts, check the clause boundary instead.

For two adjectives, try swapping them or inserting and. “Old, limping dog” passes: both words describe dog separately. “Three large dogs” does not: three tells how many large dogs. Those adjectives work together without a comma.

examples.text: The picnic group ordered shrimp, wings, and onion rings.
examples.label: Three-item list

examples.text: The old, limping dog finished the hike.
examples.label: Two equal adjectives: the switch test passes

examples.text: She wore a beautiful, silk scarf.
examples.label: Wrong: 'silk beautiful scarf' fails the switch test, so no comma belongs here

sections.tip: For adjectives, swap their order or insert 'and.' If it still reads naturally, use a comma; if not, drop it.

sections.heading: The 1-comma rule
body: A lone comma must not separate a subject from its verb or a verb from its object.

In “The beam set at an angle, created an illusion,” remove the comma. If “set at an angle” is extra information, enclose it with a matched pair instead: “The beam, set at an angle, created an illusion.”

examples.text: Expertly kneaded bread will have air pockets.
examples.label: No comma between subject and verb

examples.text: Expertly kneaded bread, will have air pockets.
examples.label: Wrong: a single comma splits subject from verb

sections.tip: Never let a single comma separate a subject from its verb. It is either no comma or a matched pair.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: When the words stay the same but commas move, name each comma’s job. Check introductions, clause boundaries, lists, and extra information.

For a name, decide whether it identifies or adds detail. For a paired interruption, cross it out and reread. Reject a lone comma separating subject and verb. Judge each full sentence rather than choosing by how many commas it has.
sections.tip: Same words, different commas: that is a comma question. Name every comma's job or cut the comma.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: restriction depends on the argument
body: Do not decide whether a clause is essential just from who or which. Determine whether it narrows a set or adds information about an already identified member.
A long subject is still one subject. Keep its restrictive clauses attached, and do not place a comma before its main verb unless that mark closes an interruption opened earlier.

examples.text: Of the twelve jars, the jars that had cracked lids were discarded.
examples.label: That had cracked lids selects a subset; no enclosing commas.

examples.text: Of the twelve jars, the jars that had cracked lids, were discarded.
examples.label: The lone comma separates the complete subject from were discarded.

sections.tip: State whether the writer means all the items or only a subset, then locate the real subject-verb boundary.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: Eric's mother[[ Louisa]] cheered from the bleachers.
check.explanation: Here, 'Eric’s mother' identifies the person before the name, so 'Louisa' is added information and takes commas on both sides: 'Eric's mother, Louisa, cheered.' The no-comma version treats the name as necessary. ', Louisa' leaves a lone comma at the front edge of the name with no closing partner, and ' Louisa,' leaves a single comma splitting the subject from its verb.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: Award-winning teacher[[, Mrs. Saunders,]] helped me become a better writer.
check.explanation: 'Award-winning teacher' could describe many people, so the name is necessary and takes no commas: 'Award-winning teacher Mrs. Saunders helped me.' Cross out the name in the NO CHANGE version and 'Award-winning teacher helped me' fails, which proves the name cannot be walled off. ', Mrs. Saunders' opens a comma pair that never closes, and ' Mrs. Saunders,' leaves a single comma between the subject and its verb.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: The group at the picnic table ordered coconut shrimp, hot wings[[, and, onion rings]] to share.
check.explanation: The offered correct version uses a serial comma before and without inserting a comma after it. A serial comma is not universally mandatory, but punctuation must remain coherent. The other choices insert a comma between and and its object, or add an unnecessary comma between onion rings and to share.
